opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to the fact that prompting is really a very thin interface to the model. When you're building a simple chatbot or a one-shot task, a well-crafted prompt can take you surprisingly far. But agents are different. They have to take many steps, make decisions, call tools, recover from errors, and stay on track over a long horizon. And every one of those steps is a place where small mistakes compound.

What we've seen is that you can keep adding instructions to the prompt, "don't do this," "always check that," "here are ten examples," and you get improvements up to a point. Then you hit a plateau. The prompt gets long and brittle, changing one line fixes one failure and breaks two others, and you end up doing a kind of whack-a-mole. You're also fundamentally limited by what the model already knows how to do. Prompting can steer behavior, but it can't really teach the model new skills or deeply internalize your domain, your tools, or your company's specific way of doing things.

So to get from, say, 70% reliability to the 95-plus percent you need in production, you usually have to go beyond the prompt. That means things like building good evaluations so you actually know where the agent is failing, collecting traces of the agent's behavior, and then using that data to improve the model itself, whether that's fine-tuning, or more and more, reinforcement learning where the agent learns from feedback on whole trajectories rather than just individual responses. That's where you start to see the model actually get better at the task, rather than just being told more carefully what to do.

The other piece is cost and latency. Often the way people compensate for prompting limits is by using the biggest, most expensive model available. If you can train a smaller model on your specific task, you can frequently match or beat the large model's performance at a fraction of the cost. So prompting is a great place to start, it's how you prototype, but I think of it as the first step, not the whole solution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that prompting is a fantastic way to get started, and it's a terrible way to finish. When you're building an agent, you sit down, you write a system prompt, you give it some tools, and the demo looks amazing. And then you put it in front of real users or real data, and you start finding the failure cases. And the natural instinct is to go fix those by adding more to the prompt. "Don't do this. If you see this situation, do that instead. Always double-check X before you call tool Y." And it works, for that one case.

But what you're really doing is accumulating a huge pile of instructions, and the model has to attend to all of them at every step. At some point the prompt is five thousand tokens of edge cases, and you fix one thing and two other things break, because the model is now weighing some instruction you wrote three weeks ago against the one you just added. There's no real mechanism for the model to prioritize. You're essentially trying to program a system through natural language, with no debugger, no tests, and no guarantee the behavior is stable when you change models or even when the provider silently updates one.

The deeper issue is that prompting can't give the model new capabilities. It can only elicit what's already there. If the model hasn't really learned how to use your specific tools, how to recover when a tool call fails, how to make a multi-step plan in your domain and then revise it when step three returns something unexpected, no amount of prompting is going to reliably teach that. You can describe it, but describing a skill and having the skill are different things. And agents, by their nature, are multi-step, which means errors compound. If you're ninety-five percent reliable per step and you have twenty steps, you're in bad shape.

So that's really why we think you have to get into the weights at some point. You need the model to actually learn from the traces of what good and bad trajectories look like in your environment. That could be fine-tuning on data you've collected, it could be reinforcement learning against some reward signal from the environment itself. The point is you move from telling the model what to do to letting it practice and get feedback. And once you do that, the prompt gets shorter, not longer, because the behavior is baked in.

I'd also add, it's not a knock on prompting. Prompting is how you discover what you want. It's the prototyping layer. The mistake is treating it as the production layer forever.

astra-6.text:
I think prompting is a great way to get started, but an agent has to do more than produce a good response. It has to take actions, interpret what happened, and decide what to do next. You can describe that behavior in a prompt, but that doesn’t guarantee it will work reliably across all the situations the agent encounters.

For example, you might tell it to verify its work. But what does verification mean for this particular task? Does it have the right tools? Can it recognize when a tool returned something incomplete? And if it makes a mistake, can it recover?

So the prompt is one piece. You also need the right context, tools, and feedback, and a way to evaluate whether the whole system actually completes the task. Otherwise, you can keep tweaking the prompt to fix individual failures without knowing whether you’re making the agent better overall.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prompting is a great starting point because you can get something that looks quite impressive very quickly. But an agent has to do more than generate a good response. It has to choose an action, use a tool, interpret what comes back, and decide what to do next. And it has to do that reliably across situations you didn’t anticipate when you wrote the prompt.

You can keep adding instructions for every failure you see, but those instructions can interact in ways that are hard to predict. A prompt that fixes one example might make another example worse. So the question becomes: How do you measure whether the agent is actually improving?

That’s where you need a feedback loop—representative tasks, evaluations, and a way to learn from failures. Sometimes the right fix is a better prompt. Sometimes it’s better context, a clearer tool interface, or training the model on the behavior you want. Prompting is one part of that system, but it doesn’t replace the process of testing and improving the whole thing.
